changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: a fictional community is considering how to explain its decisions. No learner recording or transcript has been supplied.

Invented draft excerpt:
Only when we explain our reasons people can judge our decisions fairly.

Corrected formal speech:
Only when we explain our reasons can people judge our decisions fairly. For that reason, I believe every important community decision should be accompanied by a clear account of the options considered. Publishing a conclusion tells people what will happen, but it does not explain why one priority outweighed another. We should identify the evidence, acknowledge uncertainty and name someone who can answer questions. This does not mean releasing private information or recording every informal conversation. It means giving people enough information to challenge the reasoning behind a choice. Transparency cannot guarantee agreement, but it can make disagreement more useful and help decision makers recognise mistakes before they repeat them.

Retelling the same position to a friend in ordinary word order:
I think we should explain why we choose something, instead of just announcing the result. Imagine the community is deciding how to use a shared room. People need to know which options we considered and why we preferred one of them. We should also say what we are still unsure about and who they can ask for more information. Of course, we do not need to share anyone's private details or every conversation we have had. The point is to give people a fair chance to question our reasoning. They might still disagree with us, and that is fine. At least we would be discussing the reasons, and we might notice a mistake we had missed.

Correction note: The formal opening needs can people after the initial Only when clause. The clause we explain our reasons keeps ordinary word order. The friendly version communicates the same position without fronted restrictive expressions. These two complete versions can be used for the repeat attempt.

Не используйте cleft как украшение каждого предложения. Без подразумеваемой альтернативы акцент может выглядеть агрессивным или избыточным. В устной речи интонация помогает показать, что исправляется: цена, время или исполнитель.

Устная проверка показывает прагматическую цену. “It is YOU who need to apologise” с сильным ударением может звучать обвинительно, хотя словарь нейтрален. “What I need is a little more time” часто мягче, потому что начинает с потребности. Сравните оба способа в рабочем конфликте и решите, что именно вы хотите сделать: установить факт, исправить неверную интерпретацию, распределить ответственность или попросить изменение. Dear Alex,

Thank you for your email. You describe my response to the proposal as a complaint about its cost and an objection to working with your team. I would like to clarify my position, because neither interpretation reflects the concern I intended to raise.

It is the absence of a clear approval process that worries me. The proposal does not explain who can approve changes or how conflicting instructions would be resolved. Without that information, I cannot tell which decisions I would be authorised to make. This uncertainty is the issue I would like us to address before moving forward.

I am not asking you to reduce the price. My comments were not intended as criticism of your team's ability or professionalism either. What I need is a written explanation of how approval would work, including a named contact for decisions that require escalation. That would allow us to discuss responsibilities using the same information.

Could you send a revised section covering those points? I would then be happy to review it and discuss any remaining questions. I hope this clarifies the distinction between concerns you understood me to have and the specific gap I was trying to identify. Thank you for giving me the opportunity to explain.

Best regards,
Sam

changes.before:
Illustrative setting: a failed application process at a fictional community centre.

The application process began with a form that residents could collect from the reception desk. The form asked for contact details, the activity requested, and a preferred date. Staff expected these details to be enough to arrange a booking. However, the form omitted something essential to that arrangement: the number of people attending.

The missing attendance information became a problem when staff tried to assign rooms. They contacted applicants individually, but the replies arrived through several channels and were recorded in separate places. A receptionist updated a paper list while another employee changed a spreadsheet. By the time room allocation began, the team was working with two conflicting sets of information.

Those conflicting records then shaped the booking emails. Each employee used the version available at their desk, so applicants received messages based on different assumptions about group size. The messages looked complete because they included a room and a date. What they concealed was a practical failure: several groups had been assigned rooms too small for them.

Those unsuitable rooms forced the centre to reopen bookings that applicants thought were settled. Staff had to check attendance again before proposing alternatives. The process had reached its final stage without securing the information needed for its first major decision.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: a fictional community centre proposes moving evening classes online next month. No learner recording has been supplied.

Invented draft excerpt for comparison:
I can understand saving money on classrooms. Why the change must happen next month is unclear for me.

Complete revised account for a repeat attempt:
Saving money on classrooms, I can understand. Our community centre has limited resources, and moving evening classes online might allow it to spend less on space. What remains unclear is how much it expects to save once equipment, training and technical support are included. Before accepting the financial argument, I would like to see those costs compared on the same basis.

The second aspect is access. Joining from home could help people who find the journey difficult, so I understand the appeal of a more flexible arrangement. However, we have not been told how people without a reliable internet connection would take part. I would also like to know whether an alternative will remain available for them. Convenience for one group does not settle the question of access for everyone.

Finally, there is the timetable. I understand that teachers need a definite date so that they can plan their lessons and explain the changes to students. It is unclear to me, though, why the move has to happen next month. A short trial could reveal practical problems before every class changes format. I am not rejecting the proposal outright. I am asking for a clearer account of its costs, its effect on different learners and the reason for the proposed deadline.

Editing note: The opening makes saving money the topic while keeping I can understand in ordinary order. The final paragraph first acknowledges the need for a date, then gives the unresolved question greater emphasis at the end. A clause beginning with why can also be grammatical in subject position; this edit improves the information flow rather than correcting every possible alternative word order.

changes.before:
Illustrative report: Failed customer portal launch

The launch of our customer portal failed because customers could not complete registration reliably. This report identifies the decisions behind the failure and the people responsible for them.

Project manager Maya Chen approved the launch despite an unresolved registration problem. Her approval allowed the release to proceed before the team had established whether new customers could create accounts consistently. Technical lead Daniel Reed decided to postpone the final registration test until after release. That postponement removed an opportunity to identify the problem before customers encountered it.

The launch team's reliance on an earlier demonstration also contributed to the failure. Maya treated that demonstration as sufficient evidence of readiness, although it did not cover the complete registration process. Daniel accepted this assessment instead of requesting a further test. These decisions left a critical part of the customer journey unchecked.

Responsibility therefore rests with both Maya, who authorised the release, and Daniel, who deferred the test. The failure should not be described simply as a communication issue: the relevant decisions had identifiable owners.

I recommend the introduction of a clear release condition: Daniel must confirm that registration works before Maya approves another launch. This requirement would make responsibility visible without adding unnecessary paperwork. Its effectiveness would still depend on both people following it.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: This example uses the fictional disagreement between Maya and Leo in the minutes above. The initial transcript is invented, not transcribed from a learner's speech.

Illustrative first-attempt transcript:
Maya and Leo disagreed about whether Friday was a firm delivery deadline. Maya stated that she had understood it as confirmed. Leo acknowledged calling Friday the target date, but he denied promising delivery that day. He said that a target date was provisional until the supplier confirmed it. Maya disputed whether that distinction had been clear. She admitted that the email did not use the word “confirmed”, but maintained that her team had a reasonable basis for planning around Friday. Leo accepted that his message could have been clearer, although he did not accept that he had agreed to a fixed deadline. Maya requested a written commitment, and Leo offered an update the following morning after checking availability. My choice of verbs matters here. “Admitted” can make Maya's acceptance of the email's wording sound like a reluctant confession. “Acknowledged” would report that acceptance with less implication about her attitude. Likewise, saying Leo “confessed” would suggest wrongdoing that the account does not establish. Saying either person “proved” their position would go further still, because the meeting left their disagreement unresolved. A neutral retelling should preserve that uncertainty.

Corrected transcript for the repeat attempt:
Maya and Leo disagreed about the meaning of a delivery email. Maya stated that she had understood Friday to be a confirmed deadline. Leo acknowledged describing Friday as the target date, but denied promising delivery by then. He explained that he treated a target date as provisional until confirmation. Maya disputed whether the email had made that status clear. She acknowledged that it did not contain the word “confirmed”, but maintained that her team had a reasonable basis for planning around Friday. Leo accepted that the message could have been clearer without accepting that it created a fixed deadline. Maya requested a written commitment. Leo offered to send an update the next morning after checking availability; he did not promise delivery on Friday. I used “acknowledged” for Maya's acceptance of the wording because “admitted” might imply reluctance or fault that this account does not establish. I used “denied promising” for Leo because he rejected a specific interpretation of his words. Calling his explanation an “excuse” would add my judgement. Finally, neither side demonstrated that its interpretation was correct: the disagreement remained unresolved, so my retelling should not turn either position into a proven fact.

changes.before:
Consider two ways of studying English: working through a self-paced online course and attending a small discussion class. The former lets learners choose when to study; the latter gives them scheduled opportunities to speak with other people. These are differences between the methods, not promises about the results.

An online course may offer several explanations of the same grammar point. A learner who finds one confusing can try a clearer one, provided another explanation is available. Recorded exercises can also be repeated, whereas live ones depend on the class schedule. However, completing an exercise does not necessarily mean that the learner can use the language spontaneously.

A discussion class offers a different kind of practice. Learners can ask follow-up questions and respond to unexpected comments. If a group is too large for regular participation, a smaller one may offer more chances to speak, although that depends on how the teacher organises the discussion.

For an illustrative learner with an unpredictable work schedule, I would choose the online course as the main method and add occasional discussion sessions. The flexibility of the online course would support regular study; the discussion sessions would provide conversational practice. Whether either method improves this learner's English would need to be assessed separately through their actual performance.

Illustrative starting situation: a team is preparing an online booking service.

Illustrative initial transcript excerpt:
“Our success depends of clear priorities, and we can rely to Maya.”

Corrected excerpt:
“Our success depends on clear priorities, and we can rely on Maya.”

Corrected full version for a second delivery:
“I think the success of our booking project depends on three things: clear priorities, realistic deadlines, and regular communication with the people who will use the service. We need to agree on what the first version must do before we agree to a launch date. Otherwise, everyone may be working towards a different result.

The main obstacle is uncertainty about the requirements. Frequent changes prevent us from finishing one task before starting another. I do not object to changing a plan when there is a good reason, but I object to treating every new suggestion as an immediate priority. That makes it difficult to account for delays or explain what the team can actually deliver.

We can rely on Maya to organise the work because she keeps track of decisions and asks for clarification when something is unclear. We can also turn to the support team for information about common booking problems. However, success should not depend on one person doing everything.

I would suggest a short weekly review in which we confirm priorities, discuss obstacles, and decide who is responsible for each result. That would give us a shared plan while leaving room for necessary changes.”

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: repeated problems with a shared workspace.

Illustrative initial transcript excerpt:
“The missing booking was a last straw, and I decided finding another workspace.”

Corrected excerpt:
“The missing booking was the last straw, and I decided to find another workspace.”

Corrected full version for a second delivery:
“I used to rent a desk in a shared workspace near my flat. At first, I liked it because it was quiet and I could walk there. The problems started when the management changed the opening hours without telling members. Twice, I arrived early for work and found the doors locked.

I complained, but I stayed because moving would have been inconvenient. Then the internet became unreliable. I could cope with an occasional interruption, but it started affecting calls with colleagues. The manager promised to investigate, yet we received no explanation of what was being done.

The turning point came when I booked a meeting room for an important online interview. I had a confirmation email, but when I arrived, the room was occupied and my booking was missing from their system. They could not offer another room. That was the last straw.

It was not just the missing booking that upset me. It was the repeated uncertainty and the feeling that complaints led nowhere. I decided to find another workspace because I needed somewhere I could depend on. I still liked the location, but convenience was no longer enough to justify staying. The experience taught me to distinguish between a minor inconvenience and a repeated problem that requires a decision.”

changes.before:
This hypothetical study examines whether retrieval practice and repeated reading support different aspects of vocabulary learning among adult learners of English. It addresses the question of whether a method that feels easier during study also supports successful recall after a delay.

Participants study the same unfamiliar words over a short course. One group practises retrieving meanings before checking an answer, while the other repeatedly reads the words and their definitions. Both groups receive the same study time and complete an immediate task and a later recall task. Learner comments provide additional information about perceived difficulty, although these comments are not treated as direct evidence of learning.

In this illustrative scenario, preliminary findings suggest that repeated reading feels more comfortable, whereas retrieval practice may support better delayed recall. The pattern challenges the assumption that ease during practice necessarily indicates durable learning. A plausible explanation is that attempting retrieval strengthens access to information, but the design does not establish that mechanism.

The study is limited by its small sample, brief observation period, and narrow focus on vocabulary. Differences in prior knowledge may also influence performance. No claim of statistical significance is made. Further research would be needed to assess whether the pattern persists with other learners, longer intervals, and more complex material.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: a hypothetical vocabulary study compares rereading with recalling words from memory. Illustrative draft wording: “The study proves that easy learning is useless.” Revised wording: “The study challenges the assumption that easier practice always produces better learning.”

Corrected transcript for a possible repeat delivery:
The assumption I want to discuss is that if studying feels easy, we must be learning well. Imagine reading a vocabulary list several times. The words soon look familiar, and that feeling can make us confident that we know them. But recognising a word on a page is different from remembering it when the page is gone.

In this hypothetical study, one group reread vocabulary, while another tried to recall the meanings before checking them. Both groups had the same amount of study time. The preliminary findings suggested that rereading felt easier, but the learners who practised recalling words did better on a later memory task.

That pattern challenges the assumption because the more comfortable activity was not the one associated with better later recall. One plausible explanation is that the effort of remembering helps us find the information again later. However, this study alone would not establish that explanation.

There are also limits. The sample was small, and the study focused only on vocabulary over a short period. We cannot conclude that rereading is useless or that difficult activities are always better. The narrower lesson is that comfort during practice is not enough to judge learning. We also need to consider what someone can remember afterwards.

changes.before:
For this illustrative recommendation, imagine an adult learner choosing between an automated vocabulary app and individual online tutoring. The immediate goal is to review familiar words; the broader goal is to use them appropriately in conversation.

In terms of speed, the app is the more efficient option for routine review. It presents questions immediately and checks responses automatically, so little session time is spent organising materials. Tutoring takes longer to arrange and leaves less time for rapid repetition because explanations and discussion are part of the session.

Cost is a separate consideration. Assume that the app has a modest subscription fee and that regular individual lessons cost more. Under those conditions, the app is more economical. That does not automatically make it more effective: lower expenditure says nothing by itself about whether the learner can use vocabulary successfully.

For conversational results, I would favour tutoring because a tutor can respond to inappropriate word choices and ask follow-up questions. This is a reasoned recommendation, not a guarantee of improvement. Convenience favours the app when the learner needs flexible practice during short breaks; tutoring requires an agreed appointment.

I would therefore use the app for quick, inexpensive review and reserve tutoring for guided conversation. If only one method is affordable, the choice should depend on which goal matters most now.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: an adult learner considers adding a weekly conversation group to independent study. Illustrative draft wording: “The group offers little individual feedback; therefore, it is still useful.” Revised wording: “The group offers little individual feedback; nevertheless, it may still be useful.”

Corrected transcript for a possible repeat delivery:
My position is that a weekly conversation group can be a useful part of learning English, especially for adults who have few opportunities to speak outside class. It gives learners a regular reason to express an idea, listen to someone else, and respond without planning every sentence in advance.

Admittedly, there is a serious limitation. A group without a trained teacher may provide very little reliable correction. Other participants might understand an inaccurate sentence and simply continue the conversation. Some errors could therefore go unnoticed, and attending the group would not by itself establish that someone's accuracy was improving.

Nevertheless, part of the original argument still stands. Correction is not the only purpose of speaking practice. Learners also need opportunities to take turns, ask for clarification, and explain a point when the first attempt is unclear. A conversation group can create those opportunities even when it cannot offer detailed language instruction.

I would therefore recommend the group as a supplement to activities that provide dependable feedback. This recommendation applies only insofar as participants have a fair chance to speak and treat one another respectfully. If one person dominates every discussion, the practical benefit becomes much smaller. My conclusion is limited: the group can offer useful interaction, but it should not be treated as a complete learning programme.

changes.before:
Thesis
The fragment presents a qualified case for remote study. Its opening advantage is straightforward: students do not have to travel. However, the argument ultimately separates access from learning, suggesting that removing a practical barrier is not sufficient to guarantee an educational result.

Strong objection
The text reports that critics describe this situation as isolation. To develop their objection beyond the original wording, one might argue that an available course could still leave participants disconnected from other learners. This is an added hypothetical concern, not a finding reported in the fragment. It challenges any assumption that easier access automatically creates a productive learning environment.

Reply
The author acknowledges the risk and proposes scheduled discussion as something that can reduce it. An additional possible explanation is that planned exchanges give participants opportunities to ask questions and respond to one another. The fragment does not provide this explanation, and it should be treated as a proposed mechanism rather than an established effect.

Limitation
The final sentence prevents the reply from becoming a guarantee: access alone does not ensure learning. Moreover, the fragment supplies no evidence showing whether scheduled discussion actually reduces isolation. A fuller argument would need support for that connection while keeping reduced isolation distinct from improved learning. The overall position therefore recognises a practical benefit but leaves educational success conditional.

changes.before:
Thesis
Regular practice can support steady progress because it keeps learning active between lessons. The key point is consistency: a manageable routine may be more sustainable than occasional bursts of effort.

First reason
Frequent contact with material creates repeated opportunities to retrieve it. Instead of merely recognising a useful expression on a page, a learner has to bring it to mind and use it in a meaningful sentence.

Second reason
A regular routine also makes difficulties easier to notice. When the same problem appears across several sessions, the learner has a clearer target for feedback and can choose a more focused activity next time.

Example
Imagine a learner practising polite requests. On Monday, she records a short request to a colleague. On Tuesday, she checks whether the wording sounds appropriately polite. On Wednesday, she tries a different request, paying attention to the feature she identified. This sequence illustrates how practice and reflection can work together.

Qualification
Let me qualify that: repetition alone does not guarantee improvement. Without useful feedback, a learner may keep repeating an inaccurate form. Regularity therefore needs to be combined with attention to what is being practised.

Next question
That brings us to the next issue: how can learners obtain feedback that is specific enough to guide their next practice session?

The following invented first-attempt transcript develops the fictional notes about regular practice. It is not a transcript of a learner's recording. The corrected version supplies a possible repeat, and the final section supplies a shorter retelling.

Illustrative first-attempt transcript
Today I want to discuss why regular practice matters when we learn a language. My main point is that a manageable routine gives us repeated opportunities to use what we know. We do not have to wait until we have a whole afternoon free.

There is two reasons for this. First, frequent practice asks us to retrieve language from memory. Recognising an expression in a textbook is different from finding it when we need to make a request. changes.before:
Data
For a management decision about flexible working, the central question is which outcomes should count as success. Source A states that flexible hours reduced lateness in one office. Source B states that remote staff reported more difficulty switching off. These reports concern working arrangements, but they address different outcomes: punctuality and disengagement from work. Neither statement cancels the other.

Limitations
Source A concerns one office, so it does not establish what would happen across the company. Source B describes reported difficulty; it does not provide a measure of lateness. The messages do not tell us whether they concern the same employees, comparable periods, or equivalent arrangements. They also provide no numerical estimates from which to judge the size of either change. Consequently, a single verdict that flexibility succeeds or fails would go beyond the information supplied.

Recommendation
I recommend a limited pilot before making a wider policy decision. This is my recommendation, rather than a conclusion explicitly offered by either source. The pilot should track punctuality and employees' reported ability to switch off, while recording which arrangements participants use. Management should agree the evaluation criteria before the pilot begins and review both outcomes together. If the results point in different directions, the next decision should address that tension explicitly instead of treating one favourable indicator as sufficient evidence of overall success.

Illustrative proposal: company language club

Objective and audience
I propose a six-week pilot for a small group of employees who need English for routine team communication. The objective is for participants to deliver a clear project update and ask relevant clarification questions. For planning purposes, I assume that an internal facilitator could be available; this must be confirmed before launch.

Programme
The club would meet for thirty minutes each week. Participants would practise updates, clarification, and responses to colleagues through rotating workplace roles. A general conversation club is a reasonable alternative, but workplace scenarios offer a closer match to the proposed objective. Short optional practice tasks would support employees who miss a meeting.

Resources and risks
The pilot must stay within an approved internal training allocation, whose amount has yet to be confirmed. I propose using existing meeting software and shared materials, with no paid subscriptions. The coordinator should estimate preparation time and obtain approval before scheduling sessions. Attendance and differences in proficiency are the main risks; flexible roles and paired practice could help, although they cannot guarantee participation.

Evaluation and decision
Participants would complete comparable speaking tasks at the beginning and end. The facilitator would assess clarity and relevant follow-up questions using the same criteria. If attendance is too low to sustain paired practice, we should revise or pause the pilot. Please approve the pilot in principle and nominate a coordinator to confirm resources before launch.

Illustrative starting situation: a proposed six-week workplace language club with thirty minutes of total participant time each week.
Illustrative draft excerpt: “We can guarantee better English without changing the programme.”

Corrected model dialogue for the initial defence, adaptation, and subsequent repeat:
Manager: Why should we give staff time for a language club when we have no evidence that it will help?
Presenter: I am proposing a small pilot precisely because the benefit is uncertain. The objective is specific: participants would practise giving a short work update and asking useful clarification questions. We would compare similar tasks before and after the trial, using the same criteria. That would give us evidence for deciding whether to continue. I should replace the guarantee in my draft with a testable expectation.
Manager: Even a pilot takes time. You asked for thirty minutes per person each week, but I can allow only fifteen, including any preparation.
Presenter: Then I would reduce both the session length and the scope. We would keep the six-week trial, but each weekly meeting would last twelve minutes, with up to three minutes of individual preparation. I would remove additional homework so that the total stays within your limit. Each meeting would focus on one brief update and one clarification exchange, with roles rotating across the trial.
Manager: Would that still achieve your original objective?
Presenter: It would provide less practice, so I would narrow the objective to a concise update and one relevant question. The initial and final checks would fit within scheduled meeting time. We should assess that smaller target without promising broader improvement. Facilitator preparation would need separate agreement, and if no time is available for it, we should postpone the launch.

changes.before:
In conclusion, the proposed booking system should proceed through a limited pilot rather than an immediate organisation-wide launch. The central issue is not whether automation is desirable, but whether the current arrangements allow staff to identify and correct errors before those errors affect customers. Had we tested the cancellation process before the earlier trial, we might have identified the duplicate notifications sooner. That missed opportunity supports a more deliberate sequence of checks; it does not establish that every difficulty could have been prevented.

Should the pilot reveal recurring booking errors, we should pause expansion and retain the existing booking process while the team investigates their cause. The pilot should resume only after the relevant checks have been repeated and the remaining limitations have been documented. Should staff availability fall below the level needed to support the pilot, we should reduce its scope and revise the timetable rather than transfer an unmanageable workload to the remaining staff.

For the leadership team, this approach offers a proportionate basis for a decision under uncertainty. A limited pilot will still require staff time, and maintaining two processes temporarily may create additional work. These are legitimate objections, particularly where teams already face competing demands. However, a rapid launch would leave less room to investigate problems before wider exposure. We therefore recommend approving the pilot with a named decision owner, a clear review point, and an explicit record of unresolved issues. Approval should authorise controlled testing, not imply that the system is already ready for unrestricted use.

Illustrative starting transcript — an invented first attempt, not a learner recording:
Stative verbs describe states, such as knowing something, liking something, or having something. The useful beginner rule is that we normally use them in simple forms. For example, we say “I know the answer” and “I have a bicycle.” This gives you a reliable starting point when you make everyday sentences. However, at an advanced level, you will notice forms such as “I am thinking” or “You are being unfair.” These are exceptions, so any state verb can become continuous if the situation is temporary. “I think it is expensive” gives my opinion, while “I am thinking about the price” describes an activity. The important question is what the verb means here. Start with the simple form for an ordinary state, but pay attention to the meaning when you meet a continuous form.

Corrected transcript and script for the repeated answer:
Stative verbs describe states, such as knowing something, liking something, or having something. A useful beginner rule is to use simple forms for these meanings. We say “I know the answer” and “I have a bicycle.” That gives you a reliable starting point for everyday sentences. However, the same verb can sometimes express an activity or particular behaviour. “I think it is expensive” gives my opinion, while “I am thinking about the price” describes active consideration. “You are being unfair” criticises your behaviour now; it does not necessarily describe your character. A temporary situation alone does not make every continuous form natural: “I am knowing the answer” is still unnatural in its ordinary meaning. So keep the beginner rule, but ask what the verb means in this sentence. That question helps you understand why some continuous forms work and others do not.

Illustrative starting situation: An employee asks a manager to change a rule requiring every internal meeting to take place in person.

Illustrative first-attempt transcript excerpt:
I would rather you to allow remote attendance for internal meetings.

Corrected dialogue for a repeat attempt:
Employee: I was wondering whether we could change the rule that everyone must attend internal meetings in person. Some of these meetings are short updates, and travelling to the office just for those can make the day difficult to organise. I thought we might allow people to join those updates remotely.
Manager: That's an interesting idea. We can keep it in mind for a future discussion, although I don't think we need to do anything about it now.
Employee: I'm sorry, I made that sound more optional than I intended. I'm asking you to change the rule for routine internal updates, starting next month. I need a decision before the next schedule is published, so I can plan around it. Could you confirm by Friday whether remote attendance will be allowed for those meetings?
Manager: Are you asking for all meetings to become remote? Some discussions really do need people in the room, and I wouldn't want the team to lose that option.
Employee: No, I'm asking for a limited change. Meetings that genuinely require us to be together could still be in person. For routine updates, I'd rather you allowed remote attendance. If you can't approve that change, please tell me what restriction prevents it and whether a trial would be possible.
Manager: I understand the request now. I'll review that specific proposal and give you an answer by Friday.

changes.before:
During a fictional planning meeting, Elena hears that her proposal will be postponed. For colleagues reviewing the discussion, it is important to separate what she visibly does from what we think those actions mean. She closes her notebook, asks whether the decision is final, and remains silent while the chair explains the timetable. These are observable actions; they do not, by themselves, establish disappointment or agreement.

There seems to be a certain hesitation when she begins her next question. Her opening words are followed by a pause, but calling that pause reluctance would already involve an assessment. There is also a sharpness in her reply that I would describe cautiously: another listener might hear concentration rather than irritation. Any colleague assessing her reaction should allow for that possibility.

My interpretation is that Elena is balancing frustration with a wish to remain constructive. The very question she asks next, about when the proposal can be reconsidered, gives me some reason to think she still wants to pursue it. However, this does not prove that she accepts the postponement. Such a response could also reflect a practical attempt to clarify her options before objecting.

For an internal account, I would therefore record her question and the pause, then identify my interpretation explicitly. I would avoid describing her as resentful or claiming that everyone recognised the same emotion. A certain reserve is a defensible impression, provided it remains labelled as one. Elena's own explanation could change our understanding, and the account should leave room for it.

changes.before:
Version for colleagues — illustrative fictional release process:

The release approval workflow links change submission, risk assessment, test evidence review, and deployment authorisation. The change owner submits a release request containing the proposed scope, affected services, test results, and rollback procedure. The release coordinator checks submission completeness before routing the request to the service owner and security reviewer. An incomplete submission returns to the change owner with a list of missing items; review starts only after those items arrive.

The service owner assesses operational impact, while the security reviewer examines access and data handling implications. Both record either approval or a specific revision request in the release record. A revision request suspends authorisation until the change owner updates the proposal and the relevant reviewer approves it. Approval from one reviewer does not substitute for approval from the other.

Once both approvals are recorded, the coordinator checks deployment window availability and confirms the rollback contact. The deployment engineer then schedules the release within the agreed window. If the scope changes after approval, the request returns for review because the existing approvals cover only the previously described change.

During deployment, the engineer records completion status and any rollback decision. The service owner checks the agreed service indicators before closing the release record. Closure confirms completion of these checks, rather than guaranteeing the absence of future faults. Although this workflow creates several handoffs, each handoff has a named owner and an explicit entry condition. Urgent requests use the same approval requirements; urgency affects scheduling priority, not the evidence required for authorisation.

Version for a new employee — the same illustrative process:

Before a software change can be released, several people check different parts of the proposal. The person responsible for the change first sends a request describing what will change, which services it affects, what the tests showed, and how the previous version could be restored. A release coordinator checks that this information is present. If anything is missing, the coordinator asks the person responsible to supply it before review begins.

Next, two people review the request. The service owner considers how the change could affect the running service. A security reviewer considers access and the handling of data. Each person records approval or explains what needs changing. If either asks for a revision, permission to deploy is withheld until the proposal is updated and that reviewer approves it. One person's approval cannot replace the other's.

After both approve, the coordinator checks when deployment can happen and confirms whom to contact if the previous version must be restored. A deployment engineer schedules the work for that period. If the proposed change itself changes, it must be reviewed again: earlier permission covered the earlier proposal.

The engineer records whether deployment finishes and whether the previous version is restored. Before closing the record, the service owner checks the agreed measures of service operation. Closing it means these checks are complete; it does not promise that no fault will emerge later. An urgent request may receive earlier scheduling, but it still needs the same evidence and approvals. Each transfer therefore identifies who acts next and what must already be complete.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting example: the assumed profession is software operations, and the phrase is “customer data access request approval workflow”. No profession or recording was supplied by the learner.

Illustrative initial transcript excerpt:
“The workflow approves customer data, and the manager does it for safety.”

Corrected model transcript for the spoken answer and repetition:
“In this example from software operations, the phrase I want to unpack is customer data access request approval workflow. The head noun is workflow: we are describing a sequence of steps, rather than the data itself or a single approval.

Working backwards, approval concerns a request, and the request is for access to customer data. A clearer version is the sequence of steps used to decide whether to approve a request for access to customer data. This makes the relationships visible, but it still does not identify who performs the steps.

For this fictional workplace, I will make those roles explicit. An employee requests access and explains the work that requires it. The employee's manager checks that explanation. A data owner then decides whether the requested access is appropriate. If it is approved, an administrator grants the agreed access.

The purpose is to connect permission to a stated work need and a recorded decision. That purpose and those roles come from my assumed example; they are not facts encoded in the noun phrase alone.

For a new colleague, I would therefore say that the workflow shows who requests access, who checks the reason, who authorises it, and who grants it. For colleagues familiar with these arrangements, the shorter phrase may be convenient, provided that everyone understands the same sequence and responsibilities.”

changes.before:
Illustrative fictional public statement from a community learning centre:

We cancelled Saturday's adult learning workshops after accepting bookings without confirming that the teaching rooms would be available. People had reserved time to attend, and some arrived before receiving the cancellation message. We are sorry for the disruption and for the uncertainty our communication created.

The failure was in our booking process. We treated a provisional room allocation as confirmed and opened registration on that basis. Responsibility for checking availability belonged to us. The fact that several people handled the arrangements does not reduce that responsibility, and it would be unfair to ask participants to absorb the consequences without a clear response.

Our immediate priority is to give each affected participant a definite choice between a refund and a place on a replacement workshop once its room and date are confirmed. We will contact participants directly with those options. We will not describe an alternative session as available while its arrangements remain provisional.

We are also changing the point at which registration can open: the room booking must be confirmed first, and a named coordinator must record that confirmation. This addresses the process failure described here. It does not justify a promise that no disruption can ever happen again.

Some participants may reasonably feel that a refund cannot replace the time they lost. We recognise that limitation. Our response must therefore combine a practical remedy with clearer information about what is confirmed and what remains undecided. The workshops can be rearranged; the inconvenience already caused cannot be undone. We owe participants an honest account and a dependable next step.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting example, not a learner recording
In this fictional case, the established facts are that three of twelve internal reports arrived two days after Friday's deadline; the other nine arrived on time. The reasons are unknown.

Emotional criticism
This reporting process is a complete disaster. People obviously cannot be bothered to meet deadlines, and nothing ever arrives when it should.

Illustrative transcript correction
An imagined first attempt says, 'Most reports were late because people ignored the deadline.' The corrected wording is, 'Three of twelve reports were late; the reasons are unknown.'

Corrected neutral spoken version for repetition
I would describe the problem more precisely. Three of the twelve internal reports arrived two days after the Friday deadline. The remaining nine arrived on time. There was therefore a delay affecting part of this reporting cycle, rather than every report or the entire process.

The original criticism calls the process a complete disaster and attributes the delay to people not caring. Neither judgement follows from the information available. We know when the reports arrived, but we do not know why those three were late. We also have no information here about earlier reporting cycles, so the claim that nothing ever arrives on time is unsupported.

A neutral account still needs to acknowledge the problem. Three reports missed an agreed deadline, and describing the language more carefully does not make that delay disappear. Equally, it would be misleading to suggest that most reports were late. My revised account preserves the number affected and the length of the delay while separating those facts from assumptions about motivation and overall performance.

changes.before:
Illustrative essay: A bridge to a different town centre

Imagine a town considering a six-month trial that would close its central shopping street to private cars while retaining access for buses and emergency vehicles. Residents disagree about convenience, accessibility, and the purpose of public space. For a public consultation, I would describe the trial as a temporary bridge between the current arrangement and a possible alternative.

A bridge must connect places that people actually need to reach. Similarly, this trial needs clearly stated purposes: allowing residents to assess how the street functions with different access rules, rather than treating change as an achievement in itself. Its supports would be practical arrangements for access and a transparent process for reviewing residents' experiences. Without those supports, an attractive design would not answer the objections of people who depend on convenient transport.

The bridge should also permit a return. A trial deserves that name only if the council remains willing to reconsider the arrangement after examining the evidence. Supporters should not assume that every objection expresses hostility to public space; opponents should not assume that every inconvenience makes the proposal worthless.

The metaphor has limits. Unlike a physical bridge, this policy does not connect two fixed destinations: people's needs and preferences may change during the trial. Nor does everyone experience the same crossing. A bus passenger and someone carrying heavy shopping may judge the arrangement differently. The image therefore helps organise questions about purpose, support, and reversibility, but it cannot establish whether the project is fair or effective. That judgement requires evidence and explicit discussion of whose needs receive priority.

changes.before:
Illustrative situation: Two colleagues are discussing an optional evening meeting.

Maya: Could you join the planning meeting at eight tonight?
Leo: I have an early flight tomorrow.
Maya: Have you stopped avoiding these meetings, or is this another excuse?
Leo: I do not accept that I have been avoiding them; I am declining tonight because I need to sleep before travelling.
Maya: Fair point; I treated my interpretation as established history.
Leo: I can send comments this afternoon, but I cannot attend tonight.
Maya: Would written comments cover your contribution, or would you prefer a separate conversation next week?
Leo: Written comments would work for me, provided there is no expectation that I also join the call.
Maya: Understood; I will ask the organiser whether that arrangement works.

Interpretation:
Leo’s first reply supplies information rather than explicitly refusing. In this setting, Maya might reasonably infer a refusal, but an early flight could also support a request for an earlier meeting or simply explain why Leo would leave early. The inference is cancellable: Leo could add that he will attend briefly without contradicting his statement about the flight.

Maya’s question backgrounds the claim that Leo previously avoided meetings. Both “stopped” and “another excuse” encourage acceptance of a disputed history. Leo rejects that framing before stating his present decision clearly.

Safe clarification:
Before making her accusation, Maya could ask, “Does that mean you cannot attend tonight, or would an earlier time help?” After Leo’s explicit refusal, clarification should concern the alternative rather than reopen his decision. Written comments remain a proposal until the organiser accepts them.

Maya: Could you join the planning meeting at eight tonight?
Leo: I have an early flight tomorrow.
Maya: Have you stopped avoiding these meetings, or is this another excuse?
Leo: I do not accept that I have been avoiding them; I am declining tonight because I need to sleep before traveling.
Maya: Fair point; I treated my interpretation as established history.
Leo: I can send comments this afternoon, but I cannot attend tonight.
Maya: Would written comments cover your contribution, or would you prefer a separate conversation next week?
Leo: Written comments would work for me, provided there is no expectation that I also join the call.
Maya: Understood; I will ask the organizer whether that arrangement works.

Interpretation:
Leo’s first reply supplies information rather than explicitly refusing. In this setting, Maya might reasonably infer a refusal, but an early flight could also support a request for an earlier meeting or simply explain why Leo would leave early. The inference is cancellable: Leo could add that he will attend briefly without contradicting his statement about the flight.

Maya’s question backgrounds the claim that Leo previously avoided meetings. Both “stopped” and “another excuse” encourage acceptance of a disputed history. Leo rejects that framing before stating his present decision clearly.

Safe clarification:
Before making her accusation, Maya could ask, “Does that mean you cannot attend tonight, or would an earlier time help?” After Leo’s explicit refusal, clarification should concern the alternative rather than reopen his decision. Written comments remain a proposal until the organizer accepts them.

Illustrative starting position: An adult education centre proposes banning personal phones throughout lessons to protect attention. No learner recording or earlier argument has been supplied. Both sides below are fictional practice speeches. Each side is a separate approximately two-minute speaking part; the corrected versions provide complete repeat performances.

Illustrative first-attempt transcript — objection:
Speaker: I understand the case for a phone ban. A classroom is a shared environment, and one person checking messages can distract others as well as themselves. Teachers also need a rule they can apply without interrupting every discussion to investigate what is on a screen. Those are serious reasons for restricting phones, and I am not arguing for unrestricted use. My objection is about access. A rule covering every personal phone throughout every lesson could prevent someone from using an assistive tool they need to participate. That possibility matters even if most phone use is unrelated to learning. It does not mean that every student should decide privately when the rule applies. I would support a default restriction with accessibility exceptions agreed through a clear process. Phones could remain out of sight unless an agreed use was needed. We could test that arrangement for a teaching block and record interruptions, time spent resolving disputes, and whether students could access the activities. That would prove whether exceptions work. More carefully, it would give us evidence about how the arrangement works in those classes. If exceptions repeatedly prevented teaching from proceeding and another accessible arrangement worked better, I would reconsider. My aim is to protect attention without making participation depend on giving up a necessary tool.

Illustrative first-attempt transcript — defence of the original position:
Speaker: Let me now defend the proposed ban in its strongest form. The central concern is collective attention, rather than a belief that adults cannot make decisions. A lesson depends on people following the same discussion, and a phone can pull attention into a different conversation within seconds. Even when its owner has a legitimate purpose, others cannot necessarily tell that from across the room. A simple rule can therefore reduce uncertainty and repeated negotiation. From this perspective, exceptions may have costs that extend beyond the individual user: the teacher must administer them, explain apparent differences in treatment, and respond when permitted use expands. The strongest version of the proposal would also take accessibility seriously. Before enforcing the ban, the centre should establish whether suitable alternatives to personal phones can actually support every learner who needs them. If equivalent tools are available and usable, a consistent ban could protect shared attention without removing access. I would not defend enforcement that simply leaves someone unable to participate. I would defend testing whether the centre can provide that access through other means. Evidence that no suitable alternative exists would count against a blanket rule. Until that question is answered, the proposal deserves careful evaluation because clarity, consistency, and the teacher’s limited attention are legitimate educational considerations.

Corrected transcript and repeat — objection:
Speaker: I understand the case for a phone ban. Lessons require shared attention, and personal messages can distract both the person reading them and other participants. A clear rule can also spare teachers repeated interruptions while they decide whether a particular use is legitimate. I accept those concerns and support restricting unrelated phone use. Where I differ is accessibility. A ban covering every personal phone throughout every lesson could exclude someone who needs a phone-based assistive tool to participate. This hypothetical case does not establish that phones generally improve learning. It shows why the scope of the rule matters. I propose a default restriction with accessibility exceptions agreed through a clear process. Devices would stay out of sight unless an agreed use was needed, and the teacher would know the arrangement beforehand. We could try this for a teaching block, recording interruptions, time spent resolving disputes, and whether students could access the activities. Those observations would provide evidence about the arrangement in those classes; they would not prove that it must work everywhere. I would reconsider if exceptions repeatedly disrupted teaching and an alternative arrangement preserved access more effectively. We should agree in advance how to judge those outcomes. That gives us a way to protect concentration while checking that the rule remains compatible with participation.

Corrected transcript and repeat — defence of the original position:
Speaker: I will now defend the original proposal to ban personal phones throughout lessons. Its strongest justification is that attention is shared: an individual decision to check a device can change the learning environment for everyone nearby. Teachers have limited time, and repeatedly distinguishing legitimate use from unrelated browsing can interrupt the very activity the rule is meant to protect. A consistent ban offers clarity about what participants should expect. It can also avoid public arguments about why one person is allowed a device while another is challenged. These benefits do not make accessibility concerns disappear. A defensible implementation would require the centre to establish whether other suitable tools could meet the needs currently served by personal phones. That is a condition to investigate, not a result we can assume. If equivalent alternatives were available, a ban on personal phones could preserve access while reducing the need to monitor mixed uses of the same device. If suitable alternatives were unavailable, that would be a serious objection to a blanket ban. I would therefore support evaluating the proposal against both classroom disruption and actual access to activities. This position gives substantial weight to clarity and the teacher’s attention while accepting that a simple rule is not justified if it prevents someone from participating.

Those questions require evidence that the appeal to parental responsibility does not itself provide.

changes.before:
Illustrative discussion summary

The following is an imagined summary of a discussion between learner representatives, teaching staff, and the course provider’s finance team about charging for courses.

All three parties agreed that any proposal should address access, educational quality, and continuing costs. They also explicitly agreed to commission a feasibility review before deciding whether to introduce fees. This is agreement on a process, not approval of a paid model or permission to begin charging learners.

Learner representatives would consider a limited trial only if financial assistance were available before enrolment and the application process did not itself create a substantial barrier. Teaching staff made their support conditional on protecting preparation time, feedback, and access to learning materials. The finance team required a costed proposal showing how teaching and financial assistance would be funded throughout the trial. None of these conditions has yet been shown to be satisfied.

An objection remains unresolved: learner representatives are concerned that even reduced fees could discourage participation among people who do not qualify for assistance. The other parties acknowledged this concern without claiming that assistance would eliminate it. A favourable budget alone would therefore not resolve the disagreement.

The finance coordinator is responsible for organising the feasibility review and circulating a written report within four weeks. The report will include a cost model, staff assessment of teaching requirements, and learner representatives’ assessment of the proposed assistance rules. The three parties will then meet again to consider whether their conditions have been met. Any decision to proceed will require explicit confirmation from each party; silence will not be recorded as consent.

changes.before:
Illustrative polished moderation script for an imagined discussion:

Thank you. Let me first separate the three concerns about introducing course fees. Learner representatives are asking whether people with limited incomes could still participate. Teaching staff are asking whether the model would protect preparation time, useful feedback, and learning materials. The finance team is asking whether income would cover continuing costs. These concerns overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

Let me check that I have represented the positions fairly: the issue is not simply whether fees are good or bad, but what each proposed arrangement would make possible and whom it might exclude. Please correct that summary if it misses an important condition.

I want to test one assumption behind the suggestion that financial assistance will solve the access problem. Are we assuming that everyone who needs help would qualify for it and feel able to apply? Eligibility rules and the application process could matter as much as the advertised discount. We therefore need evidence about likely barriers, rather than treating the existence of assistance as proof of accessibility.

My proposed conditional conclusion is this: we could consider a limited trial if the cost model covers teaching and assistance, staff judge the teaching arrangements adequate, and learner representatives accept the access safeguards. Until those conditions have been checked, we have no basis for announcing approval. I suggest that the finance coordinator organise a joint review before our next meeting. Can each party explicitly confirm whether it supports that next step?

Illustrative starting situation:
An editor is discussing the lesson’s pilot sentence and its overconfident revision. The transcript fragment below is invented; it is not a transcript of the learner’s recording.

Illustrative uncorrected transcript fragment:
“I made two correction. I put back may because the evidence do not support certainty. I also restored the support condition. I prefer help to benefit, but benefit are not wrong.”

Corrected model for the repeat response:
“I would defend two substantive edits to the sentence about the pilot. First, I restored the original limits on the claim. The wording ‘The programme helps learners’ presents the benefit as established and leaves the group unrestricted. By contrast, ‘The pilot may help some learners’ preserves the tentative status of both the intervention and its possible benefit. This is a correction of meaning, because the stronger wording goes beyond the original statement.

Second, I restored ‘when support is available.’ That condition tells the reader when the possible benefit applies. Without it, someone could reasonably interpret the sentence as independent of support. The extra words are therefore necessary, even though they make the sentence longer. I would keep them unless the author supplied a basis for changing the claim.

One choice I would acknowledge as a preference is using ‘help’ rather than ‘benefit.’ Both verbs can work here. I prefer ‘help’ because it is familiar and fits the direct tone, but I would not describe ‘benefit’ as a grammatical error.

In the illustrative transcript, ‘two correction’ needs a plural noun, and ‘the evidence do’ needs singular agreement. The quoted word ‘benefit’ also takes ‘is.’ Those language corrections are separate from my stylistic preference.”

changes.before:
Illustrative starting example: the two publications below are assumed source choices for this model, not sources supplied by the learner or newly verified here.

For adults organising their own learning, independence and feedback should serve complementary purposes: independence makes learners attempt difficult work, while feedback helps them judge whether their approach is effective.

Dunlosky and colleagues review learning techniques and identify practice testing and distributed practice as particularly useful approaches (https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100612453266). Their review supports organising independent study around retrieval and revisiting material rather than relying mainly on rereading. It does not establish that learners can diagnose every misunderstanding without assistance.

Hattie and Timperley examine feedback and argue that its effects depend on its type and delivery (https://doi.org/10.3102/003465430298487). Their framework distinguishes information about the task, the process, and self-regulation from comments directed at the person. This suggests that useful feedback should clarify a difficulty and inform a subsequent action, rather than merely express approval.

My conclusion is that learners should first attempt a manageable task independently, then seek focused feedback on uncertain or consequential aspects, and finally apply the correction to a different task. That sequence is my practical synthesis, not a procedure jointly tested by these publications.

A reasonable objection is that expert feedback costs time or money. I would therefore prioritise it for persistent errors, while treating peer comments as suggestions requiring judgement. Another limitation is that broad educational findings do not determine the best schedule for every adult learner. Progress should be checked through later independent performance, with the balance adjusted when mistakes persist or feedback becomes a substitute for thinking.

I help organize information so customers can find opening hours, services, and contact details. At the moment, I'm working on a sample website for a small café, and I'm learning more about making pages easy to use on phones. Could you give me ten minutes to discuss what you need? As a first step, we could look at your current website together and choose one page to review. I can't promise more sales, but I can explain my suggestions and discuss what is realistic.

В переговорах if помогает связать предложение с условием. If you give us more time, we will fix the problem — реальный план, который говорящий считает возможным. В обычном придаточном условия после if не ставят will только ради будущего: if you give, а не if you will give. If you gave us more time, we could fix the problem делает предложение менее прямым и более гипотетическим. Прошедшая форма gave здесь не обязана описывать прошлое.

Could предлагает возможность; should советует; must и have to обозначают необходимость и могут усиливать давление. Сначала назови общую цель, затем ограничение и реалистичную уступку. I understand why you are upset признаёт чувство, но само по себе не означает согласие с обвинением. Извинение I am sorry we kept you waiting относится к конкретному действию; формула I am sorry you feel that way может прозвучать как отказ от ответственности. Сравни смысл прежде, чем заучивать готовую вежливую фразу.

changes.before:
Internal report: Missing laptop

Confirmed facts and recorded accounts
A laptop disappeared from the shared office on Tuesday afternoon. The entry log records Leo's pass being used at 2:10. The camera above the lift stopped working at two. According to Leo, he collected a charger and left after five minutes. A cleaner remembers a blue bag near the door, but this account does not establish who owned it. A colleague reports that the side door was open for a delivery and that visitors do not always use passes.

Possible explanations
Leo might have collected only the charger, as he says. We cannot rule out another visitor entering through the side door. The laptop might also have been moved for repairs. The manager's argument that Leo must have taken it relies on nobody else signing in; that does not establish that nobody else entered.

Next checks
Before contacting anyone outside the company, the team will check the delivery record and ask whether the laptop was moved for repairs. These checks are needed before an explanation is presented as an established fact.

A former employee then says that the scene was planned for a camera crew and that drivers are usually given too little time to offer extra help. The company confirms that the customer agreed to be filmed, but argues that a planned video can still show a real service. Illustrative starting example — not a learner-supplied advertisement: I use the lesson's original practice text as the source for this example. It is not dialogue from the television series.

Source text:
A local delivery company posts a video showing its driver carrying groceries upstairs for an elderly customer. The caption describes the company as the most caring service in town. Within two days the video is shared by hundreds of people. A former employee then says that the scene was planned for a camera crew and that drivers are usually given too little time to offer extra help. The company confirms that the customer agreed to be filmed, but argues that a planned video can still show a real service. A neighbourhood group asks the company to publish its delivery policy rather than respond with another emotional advertisement.

Neutral retelling — spoken script:
The advertisement shows a driver from a local delivery company carrying groceries upstairs for an elderly customer. The caption describes the company as the most caring service in town. Within two days, the video is shared by hundreds of people. A former employee says the scene was arranged for filming and that drivers generally have too little time to give extra help. The company confirms the customer's consent to filming and argues that a planned scene can still represent a real service. A neighbourhood group asks for the delivery policy to be published. The account does not establish whether help upstairs is normally included, available only in some circumstances, or exceptional.

Emotions and implicit comparisons — spoken explanation:
The scene could encourage sympathy for the elderly customer and trust in the company. It could give viewers the impression that personal care is a normal part of every delivery. Calling the service the most caring also implies that competitors care less, although the text provides no comparison of their services. The emotional appeal therefore goes beyond showing one act of assistance: it invites viewers to connect that act with the company's overall character.

changes.before:
Illustrative fictional story:

Until last spring, I used to think that cooking dinner was a waste of time. Every evening, I would buy something ready to eat on my way home. I liked the convenience, and I rarely thought about learning to cook.

That changed in April, when a friend invited me to make dinner with her. Before that evening, I had never cooked a complete meal without following a video. We made a simple vegetable soup, and she explained each step while I was chopping the vegetables. I realised that cooking could be a relaxed activity rather than another difficult job.

Since then, I have started cooking twice a week. I still buy prepared food when I am busy, but I no longer believe that every homemade meal takes hours. Looking back, I should have tried a simple recipe earlier. Now I want to learn one new dish each month.

changes.before:
Illustrative personal situations

1. An itemised bill
After dinner with friends, I asked the waiter for an itemised bill because we wanted to pay separately. It showed each dish and drink, so we could work out what each person owed.

2. Spot a pattern
I kept arriving late for my evening class and wanted to understand why. When I compared my travel notes, I was able to spot a pattern: every delay happened when I took the bus instead of the train.

3. Raise a concern
The light above the stairs in my building stopped working, so I called the building manager to raise a concern about safety. She said she would arrange a repair, and I asked her to let me know when it was scheduled.

changes.before:
Авторский учебный текст, не цитата, не транскрипт и не пересказ сцены сериала:
A residents' group reviews twenty monthly bills from a shared housing service. Four bills contain a maintenance fee twice, although the wording is slightly different. Three residents say that they paid without asking because they assumed the second item covered emergency support. The group has not yet checked the service agreement, and only two months of bills are available. A volunteer proposes describing the pattern as deliberate overcharging in a public post. Another suggests first requesting an itemised explanation and asking whether the same entries appear in earlier months. They agree to preserve copies, record every response and avoid publishing residents' names.

Этот текст специально написан для тренировки темы. Он не выдаёт содержание эпизода и не имитирует настоящую транскрипцию. Во вкладке «Примеры» его можно озвучить голосом браузера. Для самостоятельной проверки понимания сначала прослушай, затем закрой текст и ответь на вопросы.

changes.before:
Retelling:
A residents' group is looking through twenty monthly bills from a shared housing service. They notice that four bills list a maintenance fee twice, although the descriptions are slightly different. Three residents explain that they paid without questioning the extra item because they thought it covered emergency support. That raises a concern, but there are important gaps in the evidence: the group has not checked the service agreement, and it has bills for only two months. One volunteer wants to call this deliberate overcharging in a public post. Another proposes a more cautious approach: request an itemised explanation and ask whether the same entries appear in earlier months. The discussion therefore moves from a proposed accusation towards checking the evidence. The group agrees to keep copies, record every response and avoid publishing residents' names. The cause of the repeated fee remains unresolved.

Possible next step:
They might review the service agreement next, because its terms could help them assess what the maintenance fee is supposed to cover.

changes.before:
Dear Service Provider,

We are writing on behalf of the residents' group to request clarification of maintenance charges. We have reviewed twenty monthly bills covering two months. Four bills include a maintenance fee twice, although the descriptions of the two entries differ slightly.

Three residents have told us that they paid without asking for clarification because they assumed the second entry covered emergency support. We cannot yet confirm whether these entries represent separate services or duplicate charges. We have not yet checked the service agreement, and our review is limited to the two months of bills currently available.

Please provide an itemised explanation of both maintenance entries, identifying the service covered by each charge, together with the relevant sections of the service agreement. Please also confirm whether the same entries appear in earlier months and supply copies of the relevant earlier bills so that we can examine them.

We would appreciate a written response by 24 September 2026. We will preserve copies of the documents and record responses while keeping residents' names out of public communications. Your explanation would help us assess the charges before deciding whether further review is needed.

Kind regards,
The residents' group

Present Perfect связывает накопленные результаты с текущим расследованием: We have checked twelve invoices. Если важны сами документы, используй пассив: Twelve invoices have been checked. В конструкции has been charged слово been — третья форма be, а charged — смысловой глагол. Has charged означает, что субъект сам взял плату; has been charged — что плату взяли с него. Указанное законченное время обычно требует Past Simple: They were charged twice last Monday.

С количественными словами различай счётное и неисчисляемое: fewer errors, less information; several documents, some evidence. A number of clients have complained требует множественного согласования, the number of complaints has increased — единственного, потому что подлежащее number. Процент без базы сравнения мало говорит: 20% of five records — один документ. В отчёте сначала укажи размер выборки, затем наблюдение, ограничение и нужную проверку. Повторяемость ошибки усиливает гипотезу, но сама по себе не доказывает намерение.

changes.before:
Illustrative personal situations — fictional starting examples

1. Undermine someone's confidence
When I was learning to drive, my brother laughed whenever I stalled, which began to undermine my confidence even though I wanted to keep practising. I asked him to stop commenting, and our next practice session felt much less stressful.

2. Earn someone's trust
My neighbour was nervous about leaving her cat with someone else, so I offered to send her an update every evening while she was away. By keeping that promise throughout her trip, I managed to earn her trust, and she asked me to help again.

3. Set a boundary
A friend kept calling late at night to discuss problems at work, but I needed uninterrupted sleep before my early shifts. I decided to set a boundary by explaining that I could talk before nine, and we agreed to catch up earlier.

changes.before:
Dear brother,

After our conversation, I want to explain why submitting a different proposal without consulting me was such a serious issue. We had already agreed on a revision process, and your decision bypassed that agreement. What upset me most was being excluded from the decision, rather than simply seeing my design changed.

Although I recognise your experience and value the professional criticism you bring to our work, I cannot accept experience as a substitute for consultation. You said you were protecting the studio because my proposal was too ambitious. I am willing to examine that concern carefully, but it does not settle the separate question of who can authorise a submission.

For future competitions, I suggest that we record proposed changes in one shared document, explain our reasons, and review both versions together before anything is sent. If we still disagree, we should ask a third reviewer to assess the disputed design choices, then meet again to agree on our submission. Neither of us should submit a version independently while that discussion remains unresolved.

Please confirm whether you agree to this procedure, or suggest specific changes before we return to the design debate. I want your expertise to help shape our decisions within a process that includes us both.

Elena
