changes.before:
Медиация здесь означает передачу существенного смысла другой аудитории с сохранением фактов и границ уверенности. Посетителю обычно нужно понять, что он увидит, куда сможет пройти и почему пространство организовано именно так. Читателю культурного журнала интереснее, какую общественную идею выражает архитектурный выбор. Различие регистров не позволяет придумывать новые сведения: меняются порядок, акцент и степень терминологической плотности. Термин лучше объяснять внутри аргумента: назвать fenestration и сразу указать, что речь идёт о расположении окон, а затем связать эту особенность с обсуждаемым впечатлением.

В публичной речи предложения могут быть короче, чем в колонке, но логика должна оставаться сложной и точной. Используйте явные переходы между позициями и собственным выбором. Избегайте административных оборотов вроде implementation of utilisation, если достаточно use. Русское «данное здание» обычно не требует постоянного this particular building: название или местоимение естественнее. В заданиях на устную речь оцениваются формулировки, смысловые связи и работа с неопределённостью. Написанный эталон не подтверждает произношение, спонтанное взаимодействие или профессиональную квалификацию. Разные обоснованные ответы допустимы, если они сохраняют факты и не выдают предпочтение за установленный результат.

changes.before:
Original teaching material. The building, people and proposals described here are fictional.

Alder House stands on the north side of Bell Square, with its main entrance facing south towards the paving and a row of small shops. Built as a municipal records office, it is now empty. A cultural centre is proposed, but no final arrangement has been chosen. The argument concerns more than whether an old building should survive. It concerns what, exactly, would survive when the public enters it for a different reason.

From the square, the façade reads as five vertical bays: five repeated divisions rather than five separate rooms. Each outer bay has a tall ground-floor window with a shorter window directly above. The central bay contains the entrance and an upper window. Pale brick forms most of the surface. Darker stone surrounds the entrance, where a shallow porch rests on a column at either side. A narrow cornice, a projecting horizontal band, runs above the upper windows.

The roof adds a less disciplined note. Its eaves extend slightly beyond the brick walls. A small dormer, containing a window, projects from each side of the roof facing the square. At the centre, a triangular gable rises above the entrance bay. None of these features is especially elaborate. Together, however, they make the middle of the building more emphatic than its edges. Calling that emphasis dignified is an interpretation; the arrangement itself is visible.

The fenestration is regular, but the glazing is not uniform. Several upper panes have slight distortions through which reflections appear uneven. Others look flatter and clearer. This difference can be observed from outside, although the age of each pane has not been established. An elevation, a straight-on representation of the front, would show the windows' alignment. It would not explain the experience of walking through the rooms behind them.

Inside, the floor plan begins with a narrow entrance hall running north from the central door. Two former offices lie on either side of this hall, making four in total. At its far end, double doors open into a broad rear room that stretches across most of the building's width. Three tall windows face the northern yard. From the entrance, a visitor sees the double doors but cannot see much of either pair of side rooms.

The front offices retain timber door surrounds and patches of older lime plaster. In the rear room, the timber floor is worn most visibly near the doorway. These elements form part of the historic fabric: the surviving physical substance of the building, not the desks that once occupied it. Their condition has not been comprehensively assessed. Wear records use, but it cannot tell a visitor whether a component needs repair or what alterations it could accept.

Designer Mara Vale proposes removing the partitions between the entrance hall and the four offices, producing a broad front room for exhibitions and informal gathering. The rear room would remain a separate space. She would retain the external window openings and the entrance porch. Her argument is that the building's present sequence makes the public behave like applicants waiting to be summoned. A cultural centre, she says, should allow people to understand its main space immediately.

Local essayist Ivo Reed favours retaining the smaller rooms and widening the range of activities within them. He sees the repeated doorways as invitations to discover something at a manageable scale. For him, an immediately legible interior can become an interior that has nothing left to reveal. He accepts that the current arrangement could confuse first-time visitors, but argues that signs and thoughtful programming deserve consideration before the walls are removed.

The same tall front windows serve both arguments. Vale regards them as an opportunity to bring a shared room into a clear relationship with the square. Reed values the intervals between them because those intervals belong to a rhythm of separate interiors. Neither interpretation follows automatically from the elevation. Nor does the available description establish how evenly either arrangement would be lit throughout the day. The windows support a discussion; they do not settle it.

Vale's proposal offers an attractive promise of visual generosity. Yet generosity is easier to draw when nobody's particular place has to remain. Reed's smaller rooms could preserve the modest pleasure of finding a corner that does not demand participation. That preference may underestimate the frustration of a newcomer confronted by closed doors. Still, before Alder House exchanges its accumulated pauses for one confident gesture, it deserves an account of what those pauses allow people to do.

changes.before:
Original teaching material. All examples refer to invented buildings. These are descriptive language notes, not legal definitions or technical assessments.

Façade: an external face, especially the principal front. Common pairing: brick façade. Example: The brick façade faces a small public garden.

Bay: a repeated vertical division of a frontage. Common pairing: central bay. Example: A clock marks the central bay above the doorway.

Column: an upright architectural member, often supporting something above. Common pairing: stone column. Example: Each stone column stands beneath the porch roof.

Cornice: a projecting horizontal moulding or band near the top of a wall. Common pairing: projecting cornice. Example: The projecting cornice casts a narrow shadow.

Dormer: a roof projection containing a window. Common pairing: small dormer. Example: A small dormer interrupts the otherwise plain roof slope.

Eaves: the lower roof edges extending beyond the walls. Common pairing: overhanging eaves. Example: The overhanging eaves shade the upper brickwork.

Gable: the roughly triangular wall section beneath two sloping roof edges. Common pairing: central gable. Example: The central gable contains a circular opening.

Glazing: glass installed in windows or other openings. Common pairing: replacement glazing. Example: The replacement glazing looks clearer than the neighbouring panes.

Fenestration: the arrangement and proportions of window openings. Common pairing: regular fenestration. Example: Regular fenestration gives the front a repeated rhythm.

Floor plan: the horizontal organisation of rooms and routes. Common pairing: revise the floor plan. Example: They revised the floor plan to connect two galleries.

Elevation: a building face, or its representation viewed vertically. Common pairing: front elevation. Example: The front elevation shows windows directly above the entrance.

Historic fabric: surviving historical materials and built elements. Common pairing: retain historic fabric. Example: Retaining the old plaster preserves historic fabric, even after the furniture leaves.

Maintenance is recurring care; repair addresses an existing defect. A retrofit introduces changes to an existing building to meet new requirements or improve performance. A new use describes the activity accommodated, such as turning offices into galleries. These tasks can overlap without being interchangeable.

Technical description identifies arrangements or materials. Aesthetic evaluation interprets their effect: symmetrical describes an arrangement; graceful praises it. Neither vocabulary nor an attractive proposal establishes safety, permissions or measured performance.

changes.before:
Original teaching material. This scripted discussion is fictional. Read it only when Exercise 4 begins. It introduces information unavailable in the earlier article.

Nadia, editor: We now have a programme requirement from the proposed centre's organisers. On Thursday evenings, individual advice appointments must take place at the same time as an amplified youth music rehearsal. The organisers cannot move either activity to another evening. Advice visitors need conversations that other visitors cannot overhear. This was not part of the brief discussed in the article.

Mara, designer: That changes my assessment of the broad front room. I had imagined exhibitions and informal gathering there. If advice takes place within it, visual openness becomes a disadvantage unless we introduce some form of enclosure. I still think a clear entrance space has value. Returning every existing wall to its current role is not the only possible response.

Leon, future visitor: I would welcome an entrance where I could understand where to go. But I might avoid an advice appointment if everyone in an exhibition could watch me waiting. The smaller rooms sound promising. Do we know whether conversations can already be heard through their walls or doors?

Mara: No. We have no assessment of sound transmission between rooms. Keeping a partition does not establish privacy. The rear room is the proposed rehearsal space, but we also do not know how much amplified sound would reach the front rooms.

Nadia: There is another practical detail about the entrance. The main door from the square is reached by two steps. A side door from the eastern lane has no step at its threshold and leads into the entrance hall. The route through the lane and the doorway dimensions have not been assessed for different visitors' access needs.

Leon: Then describing the side entrance as fully accessible would be premature. Could we consider keeping some front rooms while making the arrival clearer? I would also want the side entrance to feel like a proper welcome.

Mara: That is worth examining, although it could reduce the uninterrupted exhibition area. We need to distinguish a promising arrangement from a demonstrated solution.

Nadia: Let us record the competing requirements and the missing evidence before we recommend a layout.

changes.before:
Before the programme requirement emerged, I would have supported Vale's broad front room for its clearer arrival sequence and relationship with the square. I now regard complete openness as a less convincing starting point. Advice appointments must coincide with amplified rehearsal, and visitors also need conversations that cannot be overheard. A shared exhibition room does not obviously accommodate that requirement.

My preference is to examine an arrangement retaining some front rooms while clarifying the entrance. This could preserve part of the existing spatial character without treating every partition as untouchable. However, retaining walls would not itself demonstrate privacy, and I accept that this approach could reduce uninterrupted exhibition space.

What evidence can be obtained about sound transmission from the proposed rear rehearsal room to the front rooms during the intended activities? That information would help distinguish a plausible arrangement from an adequate one.

The entrances also need attention. The side threshold has no step, whereas the main entrance has two, but neither that contrast nor a clearer floor plan establishes access for different visitors. I would want the lane route and doorway dimensions assessed before describing the side entrance as accessible.

Its pale brick façade is divided into five bays, repeated vertical sections that give the front its rhythm. A retrofit, meaning changes to the existing building for new requirements, should be judged by evidence about those requirements, not by reassuring terminology. My preference sacrifices some exhibition continuity to retain spatial choice. It remains a preference requiring investigation. The next decision should test privacy and access before fixing the layout, while recognising that a building's character includes how people inhabit it.

That would keep some spatial character alongside historic fabric, by which I mean surviving materials such as the old plaster and timber door surrounds. It would also recognize the new requirement for private advice appointments during amplified rehearsal.

But my support has limits. Existing walls have not been shown to prevent overhearing. The side entrance has no step at its threshold, yet the route and doorway still need assessment. We should not advertise privacy or access on that evidence alone.

This option may reduce continuous exhibition space. I accept that trade-off as a starting preference, provided the next assessment establishes whether the intended activities can actually coexist.

changes.before:
Original teaching material. All people, objects, and events in this account are fictional.

On Monday evening, the team preparing the Small Rooms exhibition spread its draft catalogue across a worktable. The exhibition would show ordinary objects that had moved between homes and workplaces. There were no photographs in the draft, so each description had to establish what the object was before suggesting why a visitor might find it interesting. Nina, the editor, asked two volunteers, Leo and Ruth, to read the same page independently.

The first caption read, “A plain, sturdy bench from a village waiting room.” The bench had a flat seat, four thick legs, and no carving or painted decoration. It had supported seated adults during its working life, and its joints remained firm. Leo wrote, “Two separate claims: simple appearance and solid construction.” Ruth agreed. Nina's note said that either quality could be discussed without the other. A decorated bench could be sturdy, and a plain bench could be weak.

The next caption caused an argument: “An unusual decorative tile from a family workshop.” The square clay tile showed a purple fish surrounded by tiny orange ladders. It had been made to hang on a wall, with two holes near its upper edge. The workshop produced wall decorations as well as plain floor tiles. The fish design was unlike the workshop's other surviving designs, which mostly showed leaves. These facts explained both the object's purpose and the reason for calling it unusual.

Leo understood the caption as identifying an uncommon example of a decorative tile. For him, “decorative tile” named the kind of product: an object intended for display. Ruth read it as offering two judgements. She thought the writer found the tile unusual and also visually attractive. She was not disputing the wall display history; she had simply read “decorative” as praise rather than purpose. Nina observed that adding a comma would encourage Ruth's reading, but removing a comma could not guarantee that every reader recognised the intended category.

A third object was described as “a compact medical cabinet.” It was a narrow metal cupboard made for a clinic, with shallow compartments for supplies. Its width was sixty centimetres, much less than that of the clinic's larger cupboards. Leo bracketed “medical cabinet” in his notes and treated “compact” as a description of that whole group. Ruth said that “compact and medical cabinet” sounded awkward in an ordinary catalogue. It presented the two words as if they did the same descriptive job.

The draft also thanked “our old friend Daniel” for lending a wooden chair. Daniel was thirty-four and had known Nina since primary school. The phrase concerned their long friendship, not his age. Elsewhere, “the old cabinet” referred to the medical cabinet, which had been built ninety years earlier. Nina asked the team to keep these meanings distinct. Replacing both uses of “old” with the same supposedly clearer word would change at least one message.

Two folding screens stood beside the chair. They had the same height and consisted of three hinged wooden panels. One was blue; the other was green. Both could divide a small room. The team selected the blue screen because its colour matched the exhibition's opening panel. The draft said, “We selected the blue folding screen, not the green one.” Here the colour contrast was deliberate. “Folding screen” still named the object type; the contrast did not turn “blue” and “folding” into interchangeable qualities.

Before leaving, Nina wrote a final editorial note: “Explain the relationship before defending the punctuation.” She did not want a catalogue full of grammatical terminology. She wanted readers to distinguish an assessment from a category, understand whether age or acquaintance was intended, and see which alternative a contrast excluded. Where a short adjective group could not do that reliably, the team could spend a few more words.

Original teaching material. This scripted editorial conversation continues the fictional exhibition story. Read it only when you reach Exercise 4.

Nina: The trial readers have sent their comments. Several understood decorative as our judgement that the fish tile looks attractive. Two assumed that, because it was a tile, it could also be used on a floor. The workshop history establishes its intended wall display use, but we have no evidence about its ability to withstand people walking on it.

Leo: So a visitor might take an adjective about purpose as praise, then make a practical assumption that the caption never actually supports.

Nina: Exactly. There is also a new audience. Tomorrow's handout is for apprentice builders attending a language support session. Their tutor wants short captions with the object's intended use made explicit. Some participants are still learning terms for finishes and fittings. They will discuss the objects, but they will not install or test them.

Ruth: What happened to the contrast between the screens?

Nina: It did not work for this group. Their copies are printed in black and white, and they only receive the selected object's picture. They cannot identify an absent green alternative from that picture. We can now describe another visible difference: the blue screen has a straight top edge; the green screen has a wavy top edge. Both fold, and both have three panels.

Leo: The selection still concerned colour, then. The edge shapes can identify the objects, but they were not the reason for our choice.

Nina: Correct. Keep identification and selection reason separate. For our internal discussion, retain these two descriptions: “a plain, sturdy bench” and “the blue folding screen, not the green one.” Decide what each does successfully before adapting it. Please propose complete captions; do not imply a floor safety test or a preference for straight edges.

changes.before:
When editing a description, first decide what each adjective contributes. Do not begin by counting commas.

Independent qualities can normally be stated separately. For example, The guide gave a warm, thoughtful welcome. The welcome was warm and it was thoughtful; neither adjective establishes a special category. A comma works between them, but no comma belongs before welcome.

A different relationship appears in this example: We displayed a damaged agricultural tool. Agricultural tool identifies the type, and damaged describes its condition. Adding and or reversing the adjectives would not naturally preserve that grouping. Familiar adjective order is useful background, but it cannot replace an explanation of meaning.

Context can also change an adjective's contribution. Consider this example: An old customer helped us arrange the display. This might concern age or a longstanding relationship. If the relationship is intended, write: A customer who has visited our shop for fifteen years helped us arrange the display. This states the relevant fact without guessing the person's age.

Use the and and reversal checks cautiously: a possible sentence may still communicate something different. When readers lack specialist vocabulary, explain purpose directly. For the new handout, remember that a monochrome picture cannot communicate the screen's colour. Separate an available identifying feature from the historical reason for selecting the object.

Сначала определите направление между началом и концом, затем проверьте, не скрывает ли такое резюме важную остановку или разворот. Overall допускает внутренние колебания; steadily предполагает достаточно равномерное движение; continuously исключает остановки и обратное направление. Поэтому эти слова не взаимозаменяемы. Для неизменного участка подходят remained at и was unchanged; levelled off подчёркивает переход от изменения к относительной стабильности.

Peak обозначает максимальное наблюдаемое значение в указанном периоде, а не вечный рекорд. Reached a peak of требует величину максимума; peaked in требует время. После поворота удобно использовать before falling или subsequently declined. Русскоязычные авторы часто выбирают dramatically просто потому, что линия выглядит крутой. The monthly samples are separate and unweighted; participants may differ.

An independent fictional example illustrates the units. At a pottery club, 8 of 32 feedback cards requested longer sessions. Eight is the count; 25% is the proportion of those cards. At another session, 9 of 45 cards made that request. Nine is a count, and 20% uses 45 as its denominator. These cards have no connection with the commuting survey.

On Friday afternoon, I received a call from a guest standing outside a locked door. Several other visitors were waiting there too. I went out to find them. I immediately thought about the new map. Lea had agreed to send it, and I had not asked for confirmation. I told two volunteers that she probably hadn't done it. I did not know that this was true. I was turning my own uncertainty into an accusation because I felt embarrassed.

Sam spent the evening helping the late arrivals, although I had accused him of not caring. I saw him take people to the photographs they wanted to see and answer their questions. Lea later said that she had sent the map. I haven't seen the message records yet.

Today I still wish we had more space. I also wish I had checked the route before inviting everyone. Those are different regrets: one concerns the room we have now; the other concerns a decision I cannot undo. Tomorrow we will examine the records and write a careful report. Original teaching material. Neighbour Link, its team and all arrangements below are fictional.

Neighbour Link is a three-month pilot for adult residents of Eastbank. Its purpose is to help people practise everyday online tasks with patient guidance. The proposed activities include finding bus information, booking a library event and searching for local job information. Visitors will use their own devices and make their own decisions. Volunteers will explain steps and let visitors try them; they will not take over somebody's account or provide professional advice.

The community centre has approved one ninety-minute session each week, with up to eight visitors. Participation will be free. The room and the three-month timetable are confirmed. The centre has not yet said whether it can lend devices to visitors who do not have their own. No home visits are planned. The team must not advertise a service that depends on equipment which has not been confirmed.

Mina coordinates the pilot and communicates with the centre. Sam prepares plain-language activity sheets. You are Alex, a volunteer responsible for facilitating practice and helping to write the public description. The team will discuss a short mission statement before submitting it to the centre. The statement should tell adult residents whom the project helps, what people can do there, and how the help works. It should remain useful if a session time changes. A separate notice will contain the dates and booking details.

The current brief is a working document, not evidence that any visitor has already benefited. Claims about improved confidence or employment outcomes would require evidence from the pilot. The team may describe intended support, but it cannot promise that every participant will achieve a particular result.

Original teaching material. This example concerns a different fictional project. Its facts must not be transferred to Neighbour Link.

The Small Garden Exchange brings adult neighbours together to share practical growing skills. Volunteers organise free demonstrations using containers and common household materials. The project welcomes beginners but does not sell plants, inspect private gardens or promise a successful harvest.

Its proposed mission statement reads:

“Small Garden Exchange helps adult neighbours start growing plants in small spaces through free, practical demonstrations and shared experience. We make simple methods easier to understand and try, while encouraging participants to choose what suits their own circumstances. Our role is educational; we do not sell products or guarantee growing results.”

The first sentence identifies the audience, useful action and method. The second explains the approach without claiming that everyone will succeed. The final sentence sets a relevant limit. The statement does not need the next demonstration's date, the room number or the volunteer rota: those belong in an operating notice.

A mission describes what an organisation exists to do. A project plan instead sets out steps, resources and deadlines. A slogan may be memorable but can leave the actual purpose unclear. A useful mission is concise enough to remember and specific enough to help a reader decide whether the project is relevant.

Our role is educational; we do not sell products or guarantee growing results.”

The first sentence identifies the audience, useful action and method. The second explains the approach without claiming that everyone will succeed. The final sentence sets a relevant limit. The statement does not need the next demonstration's date, the room number or the volunteer rota: those belong in an operating notice.

A mission describes what an organization exists to do. A project plan instead sets out steps, resources and deadlines. A slogan may be memorable but can leave the actual purpose unclear. A useful mission is concise enough to remember and specific enough to help a reader decide whether the project is relevant.

Illustrative starting situation: An adult has been learning Spanish for three months. No learner recording or transcript has been supplied.

Illustrative initial transcript excerpt:
I have been learning Spanish since three months. I have been knowing more words now.

Corrected account for a repeat attempt:
I have been learning Spanish for the last three months because I would like to speak to people when I travel. I started with a beginners' course, and I have been studying at home for about half an hour most evenings. On Saturdays, I usually spend a little longer reviewing the week's lessons.

Recently, I have been working on questions and everyday conversations. I have also been listening to short recordings while I walk to the station. I do not understand every word, but I can usually identify the topic when the speakers talk slowly. Listening still takes a lot of concentration, so I sometimes feel tired afterwards.

So far, I have finished eight lessons and learned several useful expressions for ordering food and asking for directions. I know more words now, and I can introduce myself without reading my notes. Last weekend, I recorded a short introduction, although I have not compared it with my earlier recordings yet.

My biggest difficulty is remembering words quickly enough during a conversation. I have been practising with a friend once a week, and I want to continue doing that. Over the next month, I plan to spend more time speaking and less time copying vocabulary into my notebook.

Illustrative starting situation: A traveller prepared for a journey by printing a ticket and saving a map. No learner recording or personal account has been supplied.

Illustrative initial transcript excerpt:
When I reached the station, I realised I forgot my charger. Luckily, I printed my ticket the night before.

Corrected account for a repeat attempt:
Last month, I travelled to another city for a weekend course. I wanted to arrive early because I did not know the area. The evening before the journey, I checked the train times, printed my ticket and saved a map on my phone. I also wrote the address of the course centre on a piece of paper.

When I reached the station the next morning, I realised I had forgotten my charger. My phone battery was almost empty, and the screen went black while I was waiting for the train. At first, I felt worried because I normally keep all my travel information on my phone.

Luckily, I had printed my ticket the night before, so I could show the paper copy when I needed it. I had also written down the address, which meant I could ask someone for directions after I arrived. A woman outside the station showed me the right street, and I walked to the centre without using a map.

I arrived before the course started and had time to get a coffee. That experience showed me why a little preparation matters. Saving a map had not solved the problem because my phone was dead, but the paper copies were useful. Now I usually carry important travel details on paper as well as on my phone.

I had also written down the address, which meant I could ask someone for directions after I arrived. A woman outside the station showed me the right street, and I walked to the center without using a map.

I arrived before the course started and had time to get a coffee. That experience showed me why a little preparation matters. Saving a map had not solved the problem because my phone was dead, but the paper copies were useful. Now I usually carry important travel details on paper as well as on my phone.

Illustrative starting situation: This is a fictional story about unexpectedly finding a lost wallet. Neither transcript comes from a learner's recording.

Illustrative first transcript:
Last Saturday, I left my wallet on a bench near the library. I did not notice because I was carrying several books. A few minutes later, I realised that one book was still inside the library, so I went back. On the way, I saw my wallet on the bench. That small mistake was actually a lucky accident. If I had not forgotten the book, I would not have returned so soon. If someone had taken the wallet, I would have lose my bank card and some cash. Fortunately, it was still there when I arrived. I felt relieved, and I checked my bag before leaving again. Without that unexpected return, I might have spent the afternoon cancelling my card and looking for the wallet. The experience reminded me to check my pockets, but it also showed how one small accident can sometimes help us.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: An imagined speaker received advice from a friend last Sunday; this is not the learner's personal history.

Illustrative transcript excerpt before correction: “She told that I should choose one task, and she asked did I need to finish everything.”
Corrected excerpt: “She told me that I should choose one task, and she asked if I needed to finish everything.”

Revised spoken answer for a repeat attempt:
The last useful advice I received was from my friend Anna last Sunday. We were talking on the phone, and I told her that I had too many things to do at home. I had made a long list, but I did not know where to begin.

Anna told me that I should choose one small task and finish it before starting another. She said that a long list could make everything seem more difficult. She also asked if I really needed to finish everything that day. When I thought about it, I realised that some things could wait until the following weekend.

Her advice was useful because it gave me a clear starting point. I chose to sort the papers on my desk. After that, I decided what needed my attention next. I did not finish the whole list, but that was no longer my main goal.

What I remember most is that Anna did not tell me to work faster. She suggested making the task smaller. I would like to use that idea again when I feel overwhelmed, although I know that some urgent jobs cannot wait.

Illustrative setting: A visitor asks about an imaginary walking club.

Illustrative transcript excerpt before correction: “Could you tell me when does the group meet?”
Corrected excerpt: “Could you tell me when the group meets?”

Revised dialogue for a repeat attempt:
Visitor: Hello, I'm interested in joining your walking club. Could you tell me how people become members and whether beginners can join the weekend walks?
Organiser: Of course. You complete a short form and pay a monthly membership fee. Beginners are welcome, and each walk has a description showing the distance and difficulty.
Visitor: Thank you. Do you know when the group meets, and could you explain whether members need to book a place for every walk?
Organiser: We usually meet on Saturday mornings. You need to book by Thursday evening because we limit the size of each group. The meeting point appears in the walk description.
Visitor: Could you clarify what happens if I book a place but feel unwell on Saturday morning? I wonder if there is a cancellation charge.
Organiser: There is no cancellation charge, but please send the leader a message as soon as you know you cannot come. That helps us avoid waiting for someone who is absent.
Visitor: That makes sense. Could you also tell me whether I need special equipment for an easy walk?
Organiser: Comfortable walking shoes, water and suitable clothing are enough for our easy routes. We list any extra equipment in advance.
Visitor: Thanks, that answers my questions. I'll read the route descriptions before choosing my first walk.

Illustrative setting: The speaker describes an invented scene in a community centre.

Illustrative transcript excerpt before correction: “Someone must to be preparing a party, and the person outside mustn't be Tom.”
Corrected excerpt: “Someone must be preparing a party, and the person outside can't be Tom.”

Revised spoken answer for a repeat attempt:
Imagine that I am standing inside a community centre early in the evening. The main room is empty, but there are balloons on the walls, a birthday cake on a table and a large banner saying Happy Birthday. Several chairs are arranged around the table, and a coat is hanging beside the door.

Someone must be preparing a birthday party. The cake, balloons and banner all support that conclusion. They do not tell me who the party is for, though, and I cannot be completely certain that the event is happening tonight.

The organiser might be in the kitchen. I can hear a cupboard closing in that direction, but I cannot see who is there. It might be a cleaner instead, so the sound is only a weak clue.

Through the window, I notice someone approaching the entrance. That person can't be my friend Tom, because Tom is standing right beside me inside the room. I still do not know who the visitor is.

The scene seems mysterious because everything looks ready, yet no guests are in the room. I would ask the person in the kitchen what is happening before treating my guesses as facts.

Illustrative personal example:

I am learning to write short stories in English. I create a new character every week, and this creative activity helps me notice useful words. My latest creation is a story about two neighbours who become friends. To improve my writing, I read each paragraph aloud and remove sentences that repeat the same idea. changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: An adult is learning to cook vegetable soup. This is an example, not a transcript supplied by the learner.

Illustrative draft excerpt:
“First, I preparation the vegetables. Later, I make one improve.”

Corrected transcript for a repeat attempt:
I would like to explain how I learn to cook a simple vegetable soup. First, I prepare the ingredients and put everything on the kitchen table. This preparation helps me see whether anything is missing before I turn on the cooker.

Next, I choose a recipe with clear instructions. If a step is confusing, I ask someone to explain it. A simple explanation is more useful to me than a long list of technical words. I then decide which vegetables to use. This decision depends on what I already have at home.

While the soup is cooking, I taste it carefully. I do not change several things at once because I want to understand the effect of each change. For example, I might add a little water if the soup seems too thick.

After the meal, I write down what I would like to improve. One possible improvement is to cut the vegetables into smaller pieces so that they cook more evenly. The next time, I follow the same basic process and try that change. For me, learning this skill means preparing, making decisions, and using experience to improve the next meal.

Correction note:
“I preparation” becomes “I prepare” because this position needs a verb. “One improve” becomes “one improvement” because one needs a countable noun here.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: a fictional decision about a book club meeting, not a personal account supplied by the learner.

Illustrative first-transcript excerpt: “I did a decision to change the room and made responsibility for telling everyone.”

Corrected full version for the repeat response:
Last month, I helped organise a meeting for our book club. Two days before the meeting, I realised that our usual room was too small for the number of people who wanted to come. I had to make a decision: limit the number of guests or find a larger room. I decided to look for another room because I wanted everyone to have a chance to join us.

I took responsibility for the change and for telling all the members. First, I called the library and asked about a larger room. They had one available at the same time, so we did not need to change the date. Then I sent everyone a message with the new room number and asked them to reply.

There was one problem: two members did not read the message. I called them on the morning of the meeting to explain the change. In the end, everyone found the room, and we started only a few minutes late. I was pleased with the result, but I learned that sending a message is not always enough. Next time, I will check that everyone has received the information earlier.

Long version — illustrative corrected transcript for the approximately two-minute telling and its repeat:
Last Saturday, I went to a café because I was meeting my cousin Emma there. I was sitting at a table and waiting for her when a woman came over with a large cake. She put it in front of me and wished me good luck. At first, I thought Emma had arranged a surprise. I thanked the woman, but I did not understand why she was wishing me luck.

A moment later, she asked if I was nervous about the competition. That was when I realised something was wrong. I told her I was just waiting for my cousin and did not know anything about a competition. She checked her phone and started laughing.

The café owner had told her to give the cake to a man in a green jacket. I looked down at my jacket: it was green. However, another man was sitting right behind me, and his jacket was green too. He was the person entering a cake competition, and the cake was one he had made for practice.

When Emma finally arrived, we helped him carry it out to his car. I had expected lunch with my cousin, but I ended up helping a stranger with an enormous cake.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation — a fictional beginner finding photography difficult, not information supplied by the learner

Illustrative draft fragment: “you needs to balance the light”
Corrected fragment: “you need to balance the light”

Corrected illustrative transcript for the spoken explanation and repeat

Photography is a hobby I find difficult because I have to think about the light, the subject and the camera settings at the same time; when I photograph a friend indoors, the picture may look too dark, but simply making it brighter can create other problems; for example, a slower shutter speed lets in more light, but my friend's movement may then look blurred; I sometimes say that the camera needs more time to see, but let me rephrase that: the camera collects light for longer, so movement during that time can appear in the picture; please tell me if that explanation makes sense so far, especially the connection between time and movement; another challenge is choosing what belongs in the frame, because a bright object behind my friend can draw attention away from their face; I am trying to practise one thing at a time, such as taking several pictures near a window and changing only my position; I do not expect every picture to be good, but comparing different attempts helps me think about my choices; what I enjoy is noticing ordinary things more carefully, even when the technical side still feels confusing.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: preparation for a community concert, with an invented draft excerpt.

Draft excerpt: “Before the concert, I was practising for three months. When I walked onto the stage, my hands had been shaking.”

Corrected transcript for a repeat telling:
Last Saturday was the day of our community concert, and it was the first time I could clearly see the result of my preparation. Before the concert, I had been practising the piano for three months. I usually practised after work, so some evenings were difficult, especially when I was tired.

During the first few weeks, I kept stopping in the middle of the piece because I could not manage one quick passage. My teacher suggested slowing it down, and I had been working on that section separately for several weeks before the performance. By Saturday, I had learned the whole piece and could play it without looking at the music.

When I walked onto the stage, my hands were shaking. However, once I started playing, the familiar movements helped me concentrate. I played the difficult passage without stopping, which was the clearest sign that the practice had helped.

I still made a small mistake near the end, so it was not a perfect performance. Nevertheless, I felt calmer afterwards because I had finished the piece in front of an audience. That day showed me how regular practice could make a difficult task feel manageable.

Draft excerpt: “By Thursday evening, I will have pack my bag. By the time I will leave home, I will have checked the train timetable.”

My next trip is an imagined weekend visit to a friend in another city. I am leaving by train next Friday morning, so Thursday evening is my main deadline for getting ready. By then, I will have bought my return ticket, packed my bag, and sent my friend my arrival details.

I also need to prepare a few things at home. By Thursday night, I will have watered the plants and left a spare key with my neighbour. By the time I leave home on Friday, I will have checked the train timetable again and downloaded my ticket to my phone. That way, I will not need an internet connection to show it.

A few small tasks will remain for the morning. I will need to put my toothbrush in my bag, unplug my phone charger, and take the rubbish out. I will also check that the windows are closed before I lock the door.

I have deliberately left some decisions open. I will not have chosen every activity for the weekend before I arrive, because my friend and I want to decide together. The travel arrangements will be ready, but our plans for the visit will still be flexible.

Illustrative starting situation: an imagined photography hobby begun last April; the following April is still in the future.

Draft excerpt: “By the end of next April, I will have been taking twenty photographs for my portfolio.”

Corrected transcript for a repeat telling:
I have three future milestones for my photography hobby. The first is next April, when I will have been learning photography for a year. I started last April and have been practising most weekends. The length of that experience matters because I want photography to become a regular part of my life, even when I am busy.

My second milestone is the end of that April. By then, I will have taken twenty photographs for a small portfolio and selected the ten strongest ones. Here, the important thing is the finished collection. I will be checking the colours and writing short descriptions during the final week, so I have left some time for that work.

The third milestone is the end of next June. By then, I will have shown the portfolio to my local photography group and asked for feedback. I hope the discussion will help me decide what to practise next, although I cannot predict what people will say.

I will still be learning how to photograph moving subjects after these milestones. I do not expect every picture to be successful. What matters is having a regular habit, a collection I can discuss, and a clear direction for further practice.

I think regrets can be useful if they help us change our behaviour. They become less useful when we keep imagining a perfect life that probably never existed. For example, I did not ask for help when I started a difficult project last year. I wanted to prove that I could manage everything alone, so I spent several evenings solving problems that a colleague already understood. I wish I asked for help earlier. If I had been more open about my difficulties, I would feel less embarrassed about that project now. However, I cannot assume that everything would have gone perfectly. There were other problems too. The useful lesson is that asking a clear question can save time and reduce stress. I do not want to turn one mistake into a judgement about my whole character. Instead, I want to notice the same pattern before it happens again. Tomorrow morning, I will send my colleague a message and arrange a short conversation about the task I am currently finding difficult.

Welcome to our conference on learning and technology. Today I have the pleasure of introducing three participants whose work connects research with everyday practice.

The researcher who will open our morning session is Dr Maya Chen, whose recent study received a national research award. Maya, who has also developed free classroom resources, will discuss how teachers can evaluate digital tools without losing sight of students' needs.

The designer who is leading this afternoon's workshop is Daniel Ruiz, who created an accessible reading app that won an industry design prize. His workshop will take place in the studio where participants can try the tools themselves and discuss different approaches.

Finally, the educator who will chair our closing discussion is Aisha Khan, whose community learning programme has received a local education award. Aisha, who recently published a practical guide for volunteer tutors, will invite questions from the audience. Please join me in welcoming Maya, Daniel and Aisha.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: an invented account of a mentor, a community organisation and a repair event.

Illustrative initial transcript excerpt:
The organisation, that runs weekend workshops, gave us a place to meet.

Corrected version for a repeated telling:
An important person in this example is my former neighbour, Elena, who encouraged me to become more involved in my community. She never made volunteering sound like a duty. Instead, she helped me find a small task that matched my interests. I enjoyed fixing simple household objects, so she suggested helping at a local repair workshop.

The organisation whose volunteers run the workshop is called Second Start. It offers a place where residents can bring broken items and learn basic repair skills. The organisation, which runs weekend workshops, gave us a place to meet. What matters to me is the patient atmosphere. Nobody expects a visitor to understand every tool immediately, and volunteers explain what they are doing.

The event that I remember most clearly was our first public repair day. I worked beside Elena at a table near the entrance. One visitor brought a lamp, and we checked it together before deciding what help it needed. Several people stayed to watch and ask questions, which made the afternoon feel like a shared lesson. That event changed the way I thought about volunteering. I realised that being useful could begin with listening carefully and offering one practical skill.

Correction note:
I replaced “that” with “which” in the non-defining clause about the organisation.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: an invented story about taking the wrong bus on the way to a community photography class; no learner recording or transcript was supplied.

Part 1 — Simple-sentence retelling

Last Saturday, I went to a photography class at a community centre. It was my first visit to that part of town. I checked the address on my phone before breakfast. Then I put my camera and a notebook in my bag. I left home early. The bus stop was only a short walk away. A bus arrived almost immediately. I got on it without another look at the number. At first, everything seemed normal. Then I noticed a large hospital outside the window. The hospital was in the opposite direction from the centre. I asked the driver about the route. He explained my mistake. I got off at the next stop. I checked the map carefully. The centre was about twenty minutes away on foot. I still had enough time. I walked through a quiet park and reached the building just before the class. The teacher welcomed me and showed me an empty seat. I told the person next to me about the wrong bus. We both laughed. I enjoyed the class. On the way home, I checked the bus number twice.

Part 2 — Illustrative revised retelling with two compact links; possible text for a repeat attempt

Last Saturday, I went to a photography class at a community centre in an unfamiliar part of town. Having checked the address on my phone before breakfast, I put my camera and a notebook in my bag. I left home early and walked to the nearby bus stop. A bus arrived almost immediately, so I got on without another look at its number. At first, everything seemed normal. Then I noticed a large hospital outside the window. It was in the opposite direction from the community centre. Realising that I was on the wrong bus, I asked the driver about the route. He explained my mistake, and I got off at the next stop. I checked the map carefully and discovered that the centre was about twenty minutes away on foot. I still had enough time, so I walked through a quiet park. I reached the building just before the class. The teacher welcomed me and showed me an empty seat. I told the person next to me about my mistake, and we both laughed. I enjoyed the class, but I checked the bus number twice on the way home.

changes.before:
Illustrative comparison
In this fictional classroom example, two groups completed the same reading task under the same time limit. Most of the students in Group A answered the factual questions correctly, while only a few students in Group B did so. This suggests that Group A performed better on finding explicit information in this particular task.

However, few students in Group A explained the writer's assumptions clearly. Group B also struggled with this part, although a few of its students gave useful explanations. Neither group demonstrated consistent success across both parts of the task. It would therefore be misleading to describe either group as strong in every aspect of critical reading.

The results suggest different priorities for practice. Group A could focus on recognising assumptions, while Group B could practise locating information as well. These are provisional suggestions based on one exercise. A further task with a different text would help show whether the same pattern appears again, rather than simply reflecting familiarity with this topic.

changes.before:
A company should allow four remote days a week for established employees whose main tasks can be completed online. However, this should depend on reliable communication, clear responsibilities and one shared office day.

The main benefit is that employees can spend less time travelling without losing regular contact with colleagues. For example, imagine an experienced designer who travels a long distance to work. Working remotely for most of the week would leave more time for rest, while the office day could be used for planning and feedback. This illustrates a possible benefit, rather than proving that everyone would become more productive.

The strongest objection is that newcomers may miss informal guidance and find it harder to ask small questions. A weekly meeting alone may not provide enough support. Therefore, new employees should initially have more office time and a named colleague available for help.

Four remote days should be an option under these conditions, with regular reviews of communication and training needs.

changes.before:
Illustrative starting situation: I am discussing whether a company should allow four remote days a week. The initial transcript below is invented for this example, not taken from a learner's recording.

Illustrative initial transcript:
I think a company should allows experienced employees to work remotely four days a week if their tasks can be done online. My main reason is that travelling takes time, and reducing it can make the working week easier to manage. Imagine someone who spends a long time getting to the office but does most tasks on a computer. That person could use some of the saved time to rest and still join team discussions online. I would keep one shared office day for planning, feedback and conversations that are easier face to face.

However, someone who opposes this policy has a serious argument. They may believe that regular contact helps people notice problems early and learn from each other. New employees, in particular, may not know who to ask for help. From that perspective, four remote days could weaken the support that makes a team work well. This is not simply a preference for controlling employees. It is a concern about cooperation and learning. I still support the option, but only with accessible colleagues, additional support for newcomers and regular reviews of whether communication is working.

Illustrative initial transcript — to a friend:
We’ve got a problem with Friday’s workshop. There’s been a booking error, so we can’t use the room we planned to use. Twelve people have signed up, and we’re supposed to start at ten. There’s another room in the same building at that time, but it only have eight seats. That means we can’t simply move everyone there and carry on as planned.

We could move the workshop online, but we haven’t chosen that option either. I don’t want to tell people about a change before we know what we’re doing. The organiser needs a decision today so there’s time to contact everyone. I think going online is worth considering because the smaller room doesn’t fit the whole group. Still, I’m not saying it’s already agreed. What do you think we should do? I’d like us to choose an option today and make sure the organiser knows exactly what to tell everyone.

I would like to explain a problem with Friday’s workshop and ask for a decision today. Due to a booking error, the planned room is unavailable. It therefore cannot accommodate the full group as currently registered.

Moving the workshop online is another option, but no decision has been made. The organiser need confirmation today in order to contact all participants. My recommendation is that we consider the online option, since the smaller room cannot seat everyone. This is a proposal, rather than an agreed change. Before any announcement is sent, we need to decide which arrangement to use. Could we discuss the available options now and reach a decision today? That would give the organiser a clear message to communicate to the participants.

Illustrative starting situation: This is an invented story about sending a friend the wrong address.

Full version:
Yesterday, I sent my friend the wrong address for a café. I copied the address of another café and did not check it before sending the message. My friend went to the wrong place and had to walk for another fifteen minutes. When she called me, I realised what I had done. I said, “I’m sorry I sent you the wrong address and wasted your time. I’ll send you the correct location now.” I then checked the café’s name and street before sending the new message. Next time, I’ll check the details before I share an address with someone.

Shorter version:

Illustrative spoken account

We had an unexpected change to our plan for a team review. We were going to meet on Thursday—sorry, Friday morning. Thursday was the date for sending our notes, and I mixed the two up just now. The meeting itself was planned for Friday.

Anyway, on Wednesday, we found out that the room was no longer available. My first thought was to move the review online, but I wasn't sure whether that would work for everyone. We still needed to discuss the draft together, so simply cancelling didn't seem like a good option.

I suggested using a smaller room and keeping the same time. There were four of us, so I thought there might be enough space. We checked, and the room was available. We kept the Friday meeting and changed the location.

It was a relief, finding another room. We didn't have to change the time as well. Looking back, I think having another possible location in mind could help next time, although I wouldn't assume a spare room would always be available.

The corrected figures mean that 70% of registered participants completed the course. Internal memo
Subject: Proposed checks for registration and completion figures

The previous note incorrectly reported that 80 people completed the course; the confirmed figures are 80 registered and 56 completed. The completion total should therefore be corrected to 56, while the registration total remains 80. The cause of the reporting error has not been established.

Proposed check 1: Before publication, we could compare each reported total with the corresponding records, checking registrations against registration records and completions against completion records. This would help identify a number taken from the wrong category.

Proposed check 2: We could ask a second reader to check the wording of the draft against the two labelled totals, specifically confirming that “registered” and “completed” describe the correct figures. This would help identify a correct number attached to an incorrect description.

Both checks are proposals for consideration, not measures reported as already implemented.
